title: Writing Formally
overview: Formality in English is not a single dial. It is several independent choices — vocabulary, contractions, sentence length, how directly you ask — and getting one wrong while getting the others right is what makes a document read oddly. This unit separates them, covers the conventions of the three documents you are most likely to need, and settles a rule about prepositions that has been misapplied for three hundred years.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 3 corrects a rule you may have been taught.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is one message at three levels of formality.
Do the Practice. Practice 1 is the diagnostic — which dial is wrong?
Record yourself saying the same request at three levels.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
Formality is usually taught as a single scale, and that is why learners get it wrong while getting every individual word right.
It is not one dial. It is at least five, and they move independently.
Vocabulary. Ask or request. Get or obtain. Need or require. Tell or inform. Buy or purchase. About or regarding. The right-hand word is more formal in each pair.
Contractions. I'm, don't, we'll are informal. I am, do not, we will are formal. This is the easiest dial to move and the one most learners already control.
Sentence length and structure. Formal writing uses longer sentences with more subordinate clauses. That is a genuine difference and it is also where formal writing goes wrong, as Unit 4 showed.
Directness. Send me the figures is direct. Could you send me the figures is less so. I would be grateful if you could send me the figures is formal. Notice that this dial is about how much distance you put between yourself and the request, and it is the same mechanism as the second conditional in Unit 5.
And the personal dial. I think the deadline is unrealistic. It is felt that the timescale may be optimistic. That second one is Unit 10's passive and Unit 8's abstract nouns doing register work.
Here is the practical point. A document reads oddly when these dials are set inconsistently.
I am writing to enquire about the position and I'd be dead keen to hear back. Formal vocabulary, informal contraction, colloquial phrase. Every part is correct English and the combination is wrong.
So when you check your own formal writing, check the dials one at a time rather than asking whether it feels formal enough.
One more thing, and it matters more than any of the dials: formal does not mean vague, long or difficult. That is the mistake almost everybody makes, and it produces exactly the writing that Unit 4 and Unit 8 taught you to take apart. The most formal registers in English — legal drafting, official correspondence at its best — are precise. Length and abstraction are not formality; they are usually just imprecision wearing a suit.
Second pattern: the three documents.
The formal letter. If you know the name, Dear Ms Bello and Yours sincerely. If you do not, Dear Sir or Madam and Yours faithfully. That pairing is fixed and English speakers notice when it is wrong. Then: state your purpose in the first sentence, one topic per paragraph, and end with what you want to happen.
The email. Less formal than a letter even in professional use, and the conventions are different. A subject line that says what the email is about, not what it is regarding. Dear or Hello depending on how well you know them. Purpose in the first line. Short paragraphs. And no Yours faithfully — best wishes, kind regards or regards, in roughly descending order of warmth.
The critical thing about email is that it is a hybrid. It is written like speech and read like a document, which means anything you would not want read aloud in a meeting should not be in one.
The report. Sections with headings, and the conventional order is: summary, background, findings, conclusions, recommendations.
And one thing that is genuinely counter-intuitive. The summary goes first and is written last, and in most professional contexts it is the only part that is read. So it must work alone. A summary that says this report examines the causes of the delay tells the reader nothing. A summary that says the delay was caused by two factors, the second of which is recurring, and we recommend three changes has done its job.
Third pattern: prepositions at the end of a clause.
You may have been taught that a sentence must not end with a preposition. That rule was invented in the seventeenth century by people who thought English should behave like Latin, and it has never described how English actually works.
The department I work in. The person I spoke to. What are you looking at? That is the situation we find ourselves in.
All of those are correct, natural, and standard in every register including formal writing.
The alternatives — the department in which I work, the person to whom I spoke — are also correct, and they are more formal. So this is a register choice, not a correctness question, and the useful thing is knowing what the choice signals.
In which and to whom are markedly formal. In a letter to a court or a formal report, they are appropriate. In an ordinary work email they sound stiff, and to whom in speech sounds affected.
There are two cases worth knowing.
Some verbs cannot be separated from their preposition at all. Look after, deal with, put up with. The person I look after. You cannot say the person after whom I look — it is not English.
And occasionally the ending is genuinely weak, not because of the preposition but because the sentence has nothing behind it. That is the situation we are in is fine. That is what it is all about is usually a sentence that has run out of content.
So: end clauses with prepositions freely, choose the formal alternative deliberately when the register calls for it, and never rearrange a sentence into something worse in order to obey a rule that does not exist.
Go to Patterns.

outcomes.outcome: Set the five register dials consistently, and identify which one is wrong in a mismatched document.
outcomes.evidence: Practice 1, twelve items; Practice 1 is the diagnostic for this outcome; Writing 4 correction task.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can tell which part of a sentence is at the wrong level of formality.

outcomes.outcome: Follow the conventions of a formal letter, a professional email and a report.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can pair Dear Sir or Madam with Yours faithfully and write a summary that works alone.

outcomes.outcome: Use a preposition at the end of a clause where it is natural, and choose the formal alternative deliberately.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say the person I spoke to without thinking it is wrong.

outcomes.outcome: Rewrite one message at three levels of formality without changing what it says.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can write the same request three ways and know which one fits the situation.

words.meaning: Used to close a letter when you know the recipient's name.
words.example: Dear Ms Bello … Yours sincerely.
practice: Yours sincerely is paired with a name.
Sincerely, with no Yours, is less usual here.
words.starter: Dear Ms Bello … Yours
words.tutor: Say the pairing: a name takes sincerely. It is fixed and people notice.

words.meaning: Used to close a letter when you do not know the recipient's name.
words.example: Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully.
practice: Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully.
Yours faithfully is only for letters.
Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully.
words.starter: Dear Sir or Madam … Yours
words.tutor: Say no name, faithfully. A name, sincerely. That pairing is the whole rule.

words.meaning: Included with a letter in the same envelope.
words.example: Please find enclosed a copy of the invoice.
practice: Please find enclosed a copy of the invoice.
The enclosed document sets out the terms.
Enclosed is for post; attached is for email.
words.starter: Please find enclosed a copy of the
words.tutor: Say enclosed for post and attached for email. Mixing them is a small and visible error.

words.meaning: With this letter. Very formal and now largely dated.
words.example: I enclose herewith the signed agreement.
practice: I enclose herewith the signed agreement.
Herewith is now rare outside legal writing.
Herewith sounds dated in ordinary correspondence.
words.starter: I enclose herewith the signed
words.tutor: Say herewith sounds dated. Knowing a word is dated is as useful as knowing what it means.

words.meaning: The person who has signed the document.
words.example: The undersigned confirms receipt.
practice: The undersigned is a very formal way of saying I.
It is used in legal and official documents.
The undersigned agrees to the terms.
words.starter: The undersigned confirms
words.tutor: Say the undersigned is a very formal way of saying I. It is the personal dial at its most distant.

words.meaning: Letters and emails exchanged between people.
words.example: I attach the previous correspondence.
practice: All correspondence should go through this address.
Further correspondence will not be entered into.
words.starter: I attach the previous
words.tutor: Say I attach the previous correspondence. It is the standard escalation phrase from Unit 15.

words.meaning: To ask, formally.
words.example: I am writing to enquire about the position advertised.
practice: I am writing to enquire about the position advertised.
Enquire and ask are the same act.
For further information, please enquire at reception.
words.starter: I am writing to enquire about the position
words.tutor: Say ask and enquire. Same act, two settings on the vocabulary dial.

words.meaning: To inform officially.
words.example: You must notify us within fourteen days.
practice: You must notify us within fourteen days.
words.starter: You must notify us within fourteen
words.tutor: Say notify and tell. Notify implies an obligation and a record.

words.meaning: To send something on to somebody else.
words.example: I have forwarded your enquiry to the department concerned.
practice: I have forwarded your enquiry to the department concerned.
Please forward it to the correct address.
words.starter: I have forwarded your enquiry to the department
words.tutor: Say forwarded to the department concerned. Concerned after the noun is a formal habit.

words.meaning: To add something at the end of a document.
words.example: The figures are appended for reference.
practice: The figures are appended for reference.
words.starter: The figures are appended for
words.tutor: Say append and appendix. One is the verb and one is the section.

words.meaning: To act in accordance with a rule or request.
words.example: The site does not comply with the current standard.
practice: The site does not comply with the current standard.
words.starter: The site does not comply with the current
words.tutor: Notice comply with, never comply to. Say it three times.

words.meaning: To stop yourself from doing something. Formal.
words.example: Please refrain from using this entrance.
practice: Please refrain from using this entrance.
Staff are asked to refrain from smoking.
Refrain is the formal version of do not.
words.starter: Please refrain from using this
words.tutor: Notice refrain from takes -ing. Say refrain from doing something.

words.meaning: A short statement of the main points, placed first.
words.example: The summary is written last and read first.
practice: The summary is written last and read first.
A summary that only says what the report is about has failed.
The summary runs to half a page.
Read the summary and the recommendations.
words.starter: The summary is written last and read
words.tutor: Say written last and read first. It is the most useful fact about reports.

words.meaning: How the work was done.
words.example: The methodology is set out in section 2.
practice: The methodology is set out in section 2.
The methodology has a stated limitation.
Methodology is not the same as method.
The methodology determines what the findings can support.
words.starter: The methodology is set out in section
words.tutor: Say the methodology determines what the findings can support. That connects to Unit 17.

words.meaning: Additional material placed at the end.
words.example: The raw figures are in Appendix B.
practice: The raw figures are in Appendix B.
See the appendix for the full data.
Nothing important should be only in an appendix.
words.starter: The raw figures are in Appendix
words.tutor: Say appendix and appendices. The plural is irregular and it appears often.

words.meaning: A proposed action, based on the findings.
words.example: There are three recommendations, in order of priority.
practice: There are three recommendations, in order of priority.
words.starter: There are three recommendations, in order of
words.tutor: Say recommendations must follow from findings. A recommendation with no finding behind it is an opinion.

words.meaning: What the work covered and did not cover.
words.example: The scope excluded the northern sites.
practice: The scope excluded the northern sites.
That is outside the scope of this report.
The scope was agreed in advance.
State the scope before the findings.
words.starter: The scope excluded the northern
words.tutor: Say state the scope before the findings. What was not examined shapes everything.

words.meaning: The task or authority somebody has been given.
words.example: That falls outside our remit.
practice: The remit was set by the board.
Our remit does not extend to costs.
words.starter: That falls outside our
words.tutor: Say outside our remit. It is how a report declines a question politely.

words.meaning: By this document or statement.
words.example: We hereby confirm receipt.
practice: It sounds absurd in an email.
words.starter: We hereby confirm
words.tutor: Say hereby sounds absurd in an email. Knowing where a word does not belong matters.

words.meaning: By which; through which.
words.example: An arrangement whereby costs are shared.
practice: An arrangement whereby costs are shared.
A system whereby each site reports separately.
The clause whereby liability is limited.
Whereby is formal but not absurd.
A scheme whereby staff may apply.
words.starter: An arrangement whereby costs are
words.tutor: Say an arrangement whereby. It is formal and still usable in ordinary reports.

words.meaning: In that place or document.
words.example: The agreement and the obligations set out therein.
practice: The agreement and the obligations set out therein.
The report and the findings therein.
words.starter: The agreement and the obligations set out
words.tutor: Say therein lies the difficulty. It survives as a fixed phrase outside legal writing.

words.meaning: Mentioned earlier in the same document.
words.example: The aforementioned clause applies.
practice: Aforementioned is heavy and often unnecessary.
words.starter: The aforementioned clause
words.tutor: Say that clause instead of the aforementioned clause. Usually it is enough.

words.meaning: In spite of.
words.example: Notwithstanding clause 4, the deadline stands.
words.starter: Notwithstanding clause 4, the deadline
words.tutor: Say notwithstanding and despite, from Unit 6. Same meaning, opposite ends of the dial.

words.meaning: In accordance with. Used as pursuant to.
words.example: Pursuant to clause 6, notice is hereby given.
practice: Pursuant to clause 6, notice is hereby given.
words.starter: Pursuant to clause 6, notice is hereby
words.tutor: Say pursuant to and under. Under clause 6 says the same thing and is readable.

words.meaning: Belonging to ordinary informal speech.
words.example: That phrase is colloquial and does not belong here.
practice: That phrase is colloquial and does not belong here.
Colloquial in a report is a register error.
words.starter: That phrase is colloquial and does not belong
words.tutor: Say colloquial is not incorrect. It is a register judgement, not a grammar one.

words.meaning: The level of formality appropriate to a situation.
words.example: The vocabulary is right and the register is wrong.
practice: The vocabulary is right and the register is wrong.
Match the register to the reader.
A register error is not a grammar error.
Which register does this call for?
words.starter: The vocabulary is right and the register is
words.tutor: Say a register error is not a grammar error. That distinction is the whole unit.

words.meaning: Specialist vocabulary that outsiders do not understand.
words.example: Jargon is efficient among specialists and excluding elsewhere.
practice: Jargon is efficient among specialists and excluding elsewhere.
The report is full of jargon.
Jargon is not the same as formality.
Avoid jargon with a general reader.
words.starter: Jargon is efficient among specialists and excluding
words.tutor: Say some jargon is genuinely precise. It is not automatically a fault.

words.meaning: Using more words than necessary.
words.example: The letter is formal and verbose, which are different faults.
practice: The letter is formal and verbose, which are different faults.
words.starter: The letter is formal and verbose, which are different
words.tutor: Say formality does not require verbosity. Most people believe it does.

words.meaning: Clear and simple, without unnecessary complication.
words.example: Plain English is compatible with formal English.
practice: Plain English is compatible with formal English.
A plain statement of the position.
words.starter: Plain English is compatible with formal
words.tutor: Say plain does not mean informal. That is the sentence this whole group exists for.

readings.title: Five Dials, Not One
readings.passage:
Formality is usually taught as a single scale, and that is why learners get it wrong while getting every individual word right.
It is at least five separate choices, and they move independently.
Vocabulary. Ask or request. Get or obtain. Need or require. Tell or inform. Buy or purchase. About or regarding.
Contractions. I'm, don't, we'll are informal. I am, do not, we will are formal. This is the easiest dial to move.
Sentence structure. Formal writing uses longer sentences with more subordinate clauses. That is a real difference, and it is also where formal writing most often goes wrong.
Directness. Send me the figures. Could you send me the figures. I would be grateful if you could send me the figures. Each step puts more distance between you and the request — the same mechanism as the second conditional in Unit 5.
And the personal dial. I think the deadline is unrealistic. It is felt that the timescale may be optimistic. That second version is Unit 10's passive and Unit 8's abstract nouns doing register work.
Here is what goes wrong.
I am writing to enquire about the position and I'd be dead keen to hear back.
Formal vocabulary, informal contraction, colloquial phrase. Every part is correct English. The combination is not, and a reader notices immediately without necessarily being able to say why.
So check the dials one at a time rather than asking whether something feels formal enough.
And one thing that matters more than all five: formal does not mean long, vague or difficult.
That belief produces exactly the writing Units 4 and 8 taught you to take apart — nested clauses, abstract nouns, no agents. The most formal English there is, at its best, is precise. Length and abstraction are not formality. They are usually imprecision wearing a suit.

readings.title: The Preposition Rule That Never Existed
readings.passage:
You may have been taught that a sentence must not end with a preposition.
That rule was invented in the seventeenth century by writers who admired Latin and thought English should behave like it. Latin genuinely cannot end a sentence that way. English always has, and every major writer in the language has done it.
The department I work in.
The person I spoke to.
What are you looking at?
That is the situation we find ourselves in.
All correct, all natural, all standard in formal writing as well as informal.
The alternatives exist and they are also correct. The department in which I work. The person to whom I spoke. These are markedly more formal, and that is the point — this is a register choice, not a correctness question.
In which and to whom belong in legal drafting, formal reports and letters to institutions. In an ordinary work email they sound stiff, and to whom in speech sounds affected to most listeners.
Two cases are worth knowing.
Some verbs cannot be separated from their preposition at all. Look after, deal with, put up with, come across. The person I look after is the only available version — the person after whom I look is not English, because look after is a single unit of meaning rather than a verb plus a preposition.
And occasionally a clause ending in a preposition is genuinely weak — not because of the preposition, but because the sentence has nothing left in it. That is the situation we are in is fine. That is what it is all about usually means the writer has run out of content. The preposition is not the problem; the emptiness is.
So: end clauses with prepositions freely. Choose in which and to whom deliberately, when the register calls for it. And never rearrange a sentence into something worse to obey a rule that has never described the language.

readings.title: The Same Request, Three Ways
readings.setting: The same person asking the same thing of three different readers on the same afternoon.
readings.passage:
TO A CLOSE COLLEAGUE

  Hi Sam - any chance you could dig out
  the March figures for the Eastbourne
  bay? Need them for Thursday. Ta.

-----------------------------------------

  TO A COLLEAGUE IN ANOTHER DEPARTMENT

  Subject: March figures - Eastbourne bay

  Hello Priya,

  I'm putting together the quarterly
  summary and I need the March throughput
  figures for the Eastbourne bay.

  Would you be able to send them over by
  Wednesday? Thursday is when the summary
  goes to the board.

  Thanks very much,
  Dani

-----------------------------------------

  TO AN EXTERNAL BODY

  Dear Sir or Madam,

  I am writing to request the throughput
  data recorded at the Eastbourne facility
  for the month of March.

  The information is required in
  connection with a quarterly review, and
  I would be grateful to receive it by
  Wednesday 26 April.

  Please confirm whether any charge
  applies. I enclose a copy of our
  registration for reference.

  Yours faithfully,
  D. Okonkwo

comprehension.a: Vocabulary, contractions, sentence structure, directness, and how personal the writing is.
comprehension.why: They move independently, which is why a document can be wrong while every individual word is right.

comprehension.q: Why does I am writing to enquire about the position and I'd be dead keen to hear back read badly?
comprehension.a: Because three dials are set differently — formal vocabulary, an informal contraction, and a colloquial phrase. Every part is correct English and the combination is not.
comprehension.why: A reader notices immediately and usually cannot say why, which is exactly what makes checking the dials one at a time useful.

comprehension.q: What does the text say formality is not?
comprehension.a: Long, vague or difficult. The most formal English at its best is precise, and length and abstraction are usually imprecision rather than formality.
comprehension.why: This belief produces the writing Units 4 and 8 taught learners to take apart, so naming it here closes the loop.

comprehension.q: Where did the preposition rule come from?
comprehension.a: It was invented in the seventeenth century by writers who admired Latin and thought English should behave like it. Latin cannot end a sentence that way; English always has.
comprehension.why: Knowing a rule is invented rather than descriptive is what allows a learner to stop obeying it without anxiety.

comprehension.q: What kind of choice is the person I spoke to against the person to whom I spoke?
comprehension.a: A register choice, not a correctness question. Both are correct; to whom is markedly more formal.
comprehension.why: Framing it as register rather than rightness is what makes the decision usable in real writing.

comprehension.q: Why can you not say the person after whom I look?
comprehension.a: Because look after is a single unit of meaning rather than a verb plus a preposition, so it cannot be separated.
comprehension.why: It is a genuine constraint, unlike the invented rule, and it applies to deal with, put up with and come across too.

comprehension.q: Compare the three openings and closings. What changes?
comprehension.a: Hi Sam with no closing beyond Ta; Hello Priya with Thanks very much and a name; Dear Sir or Madam with Yours faithfully and initials rather than a first name.
comprehension.why: The openings and closings move together with everything else, and the third pairing is the fixed one that English speakers notice.

comprehension.q: Find the same request in all three and say how the directness dial moves.
comprehension.a: Any chance you could dig out; would you be able to send them over; I would be grateful to receive it. Each version puts more distance between the writer and the request.
comprehension.why: The content is identical in all three, which isolates directness as one dial moving independently of the others.

comprehension.q: The third version contains something the other two do not. What, and why?
comprehension.a: It asks whether any charge applies and encloses a registration copy. An external body may charge and may need to verify who is asking, neither of which applies to a colleague.
comprehension.why: Register is not only about tone — the formal version genuinely has more to do, and the extra content is a consequence of the relationship rather than of the style.

comprehension.q: The first version uses contractions and the third uses none. Is the third better writing?
comprehension.a: No, only differently pitched. The first is entirely appropriate to a close colleague and would be wrong to an external body, and the third would read as cold and strange sent to Sam.
comprehension.why: Learners often treat the most formal version as the safest. It is not — a register that is too formal for the relationship is as noticeable as one that is too casual.

grammar.title: The five dials
grammar.explanation: Formality is not one scale. It is five independent choices, which is why a document can read oddly while every individual word is correct.
grammar.rule:
1  VOCABULARY
     ask/request   get/obtain
     need/require  tell/inform
     buy/purchase  about/regarding

2  CONTRACTIONS
     I'm, don't, we'll   informal
     I am, do not, we will  formal

3  SENTENCE STRUCTURE
     formal = longer, more subordinate
     clauses. (But see Unit 4.)

4  DIRECTNESS
     Send me the figures.
     Could you send me the figures?
     I would be grateful if you could...
     ^ each step adds distance.

5  PERSONAL
     I think the deadline is unrealistic.
     It is felt that the timescale may
     be optimistic.
     ^ Unit 10's passive + Unit 8's
       abstract nouns doing register work.

THEY MOVE INDEPENDENTLY.
  \"I am writing to enquire... and I'd be
   dead keen to hear back.\"
  three dials, three settings. Wrong.

FORMAL IS NOT LONG, VAGUE OR DIFFICULT.
  Length and abstraction are usually
  imprecision wearing a suit.
grammar.workedExample:
You need figures from somebody at another organisation.
1. Vocabulary. Ask becomes request. Get becomes obtain or receive. About becomes regarding or in connection with.
2. Contractions. I'm becomes I am. Don't becomes do not.
3. Structure. Combine short sentences where it helps: the information is required in connection with a quarterly review, and I would be grateful to receive it by Wednesday.
4. Directness. Move from can you send to I would be grateful to receive.
5. Personal. Keep I here — an external request from a named person is normal and removing yourself entirely would be odd.
Result: I am writing to request the throughput data for March. The information is required in connection with a quarterly review, and I would be grateful to receive it by Wednesday 26 April.
Now check consistency. Any contractions? No. Any colloquial phrase? No. Any dial left at the wrong setting? No.
That last check is the whole method: go through the five, one at a time, rather than asking whether it feels formal.
grammar.mistake: Setting one dial and not the others, which produces sentences like I am writing to enquire and I'd be dead keen. The other error is the belief that formal means long — this produces nested clauses and abstract nouns, and it makes writing less precise rather than more professional. Formality and clarity are independent, and the best formal writing is both.
grammar.tip: Five dials, checked one at a time. Formal is not long or vague.
grammar.practice:
Move each sentence up one level of formality, and say which dial you moved.
1. Can you send me the figures?
2. I'm writing about the job.
3. We need to get the data.
4. Tell us if anything changes.
5. I think the deadline is unrealistic.
6. Thanks for getting back to me so quick.
grammar.answers:
1. Could you send me the figures? — directness. Or: I would be grateful if you could send me the figures — directness, further.
2. I am writing regarding the position. — contractions and vocabulary.
3. We are required to obtain the data. — vocabulary, and the personal dial by using are required.
4. Please notify us of any change. — vocabulary and directness.
5. It may be that the timescale is optimistic. — the personal dial, using Unit 10's passive-like construction.
6. Thank you for your prompt reply. — vocabulary, contraction of thanks, and the colloquial so quick.
Number 6 needed three dials moved at once, which is why the original reads as a mixture.
Number 5 is worth noticing: it became less direct and also less clear about whose view it is, which is a real cost of that dial and worth paying only when you mean it.

grammar.title: The letter, the email and the report
grammar.explanation: Three documents with three sets of conventions. Most of it is fixed and learnable, and one point about reports is genuinely counter-intuitive.
grammar.rule:
THE FORMAL LETTER
  name known:   Dear Ms Bello
                Yours SINCERELY
  name unknown: Dear Sir or Madam
                Yours FAITHFULLY
  ^ fixed. People notice.

  purpose in the first sentence
  one topic per paragraph
  enclosed (post) / attached (email)

THE EMAIL
  subject line: what it is ABOUT
  purpose in the first line
  closings: best wishes / kind regards /
    regards   (warm -> neutral)
  NEVER Yours faithfully.

  Written like speech, read like a
  document.

THE REPORT
  summary, background, findings,
  conclusions, recommendations

  THE SUMMARY IS WRITTEN LAST AND READ
  FIRST - often it is ALL that is read.
     "This report examines the causes"
     tells you nothing.
     "The delay had two causes, one of
      which recurs; three changes are
      recommended" has done its job.
grammar.workedExample:
You are writing to an organisation and you do not know who will read it.
1. No name, so: Dear Sir or Madam. That fixes the closing as Yours faithfully — the pairing is not optional.
2. Purpose in the first sentence: I am writing to request the throughput data for March.
3. One topic per paragraph. The request, then the reason and the date, then the administrative question about charges.
4. End with what you want: please confirm whether any charge applies.
5. Enclosed, not attached, because it is a letter.
Now the report summary, which is where people go wrong.
1. Write everything else first.
2. Then ask: if somebody reads only this, what must they know?
3. Not what the report is about — what it found and what should happen.
4. The delay had two causes, one of which recurs. Three changes are recommended, of which the second requires funding.
That summary can be acted on by somebody who reads nothing else, which is the realistic case.
grammar.mistake: Pairing Dear Sir or Madam with Yours sincerely, or a name with Yours faithfully. It is a small error and it is highly visible to anybody who writes letters regularly. The other, more costly error is a report summary that describes the report rather than reporting the findings — this report examines the causes is a table of contents in a sentence, and the summary is often the only part read.
grammar.tip: Name takes sincerely; no name takes faithfully. Write the summary last.
grammar.practice:
Answer each in a full sentence.
1. You know the name. Which opening and closing?
2. You do not know the name. Which opening and closing?
3. What closes a professional email?
4. What goes in an email subject line?
5. What is the conventional order of report sections?
6. Write a one-sentence summary that would work if nothing else were read.
grammar.answers:
1. Dear Ms Bello, closing Yours sincerely.
2. Dear Sir or Madam, closing Yours faithfully.
3. Best wishes, kind regards or regards — never Yours faithfully.
4. What the email is about, specifically enough to be found later: March figures — Eastbourne bay, not Query.
5. Summary, background, findings, conclusions, recommendations.
6. Model: The delay had two causes, one of which recurs; three changes are recommended, of which the second requires funding.
Number 6 is the test. Compare it with this report examines the causes of the delay, which describes the document rather than reporting anything, and would leave a reader who read only the summary knowing nothing at all.

grammar.title: Prepositions at the end
grammar.explanation: A rule you may have been taught, which was invented in the seventeenth century and has never described English. What replaces it is a register choice.
grammar.rule:
THE RULE DOES NOT EXIST
  invented in the 1600s by writers who
  thought English should behave like Latin.
  Latin cannot do it. English always has.

  The department I work in.
  The person I spoke to.
  What are you looking at?
  ^ all correct, including in formal
    writing.

IT IS A REGISTER CHOICE
  the department IN WHICH I work
  the person TO WHOM I spoke
  ^ markedly more formal.

  legal drafting, formal reports ->
    appropriate
  ordinary work email -> stiff
  speech -> "to whom" sounds affected

TWO REAL CONSTRAINTS

  1 some verbs CANNOT be separated
      look after, deal with, put up with,
      come across
      "the person I look after" only.

  2 sometimes the ending is weak because
    the SENTENCE is empty, not because of
    the preposition.

NEVER rearrange into something worse to
obey a rule that does not exist.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to refer to a department where you work, in an email to a colleague.
1. The natural version: the department I work in.
2. Is it correct? Yes, entirely, and it always has been.
3. Does the register call for the formal alternative? An email to a colleague does not. The department in which I work would read as stiff.
4. So use the natural version.
Now a formal report for an external body.
1. Same content: the department in which the incident occurred.
2. Here the formal version fits the surrounding register, and the sentence around it is already using longer structures.
3. Both are correct; the choice follows the document.
And a case where you have no choice. You want to refer to somebody you care for.
1. The verb is look after, which is a single unit of meaning.
2. The person after whom I look is not English.
3. So: the person I look after. There is no formal alternative to reach for, and rearranging would produce nonsense.
That third case is why the invented rule is actively harmful — obeying it sometimes forces a writer into a sentence that is worse or not English at all.
grammar.mistake: Rearranging a natural sentence into a worse one to obey a rule that does not exist. This is the commonest consequence, and it produces stiff writing in registers that do not call for it. The opposite error is using to whom in speech or in an ordinary email, where it sounds affected rather than educated.
grammar.tip: End with a preposition freely. Choose in which and to whom deliberately.
grammar.practice:
Write the natural version and, where possible, the formal alternative. Mark any where there is no alternative.
1. The department I work in.
2. The person I spoke to.
3. The person I look after.
4. The problem we are dealing with.
5. The situation we find ourselves in.
6. The colleague I came across the report through.
grammar.answers:
1. The department I work in. / The department in which I work.
2. The person I spoke to. / The person to whom I spoke.
3. The person I look after. — NO ALTERNATIVE; look after cannot be separated.
4. The problem we are dealing with. — NO ALTERNATIVE; deal with cannot be separated.
5. The situation we find ourselves in. / The situation in which we find ourselves.
6. The colleague through whom I came across the report is awkward; better to rewrite entirely — a colleague showed me the report. — come across cannot be separated, and number 6 shows that the fix is sometimes to write a different sentence.
Numbers 3, 4 and 6 have no formal alternative, which is the practical argument against the invented rule: obeying it would force you into something that is not English.
Numbers 1, 2 and 5 have genuine alternatives, and choosing between them is a register decision about the document you are writing.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Move one dial
speaking.instructions:
Take six sentences and say each one twice — once informal and once formal — but change only one dial each time.
First vocabulary only. Then contractions only. Then directness only.
Record eighteen sentences in total.
Changing one dial at a time makes each one audible on its own, which is what the check in card 1 depends on.
speaking.tutor: Say six sentences and ask the tutor to raise the formality of one dial only.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Which dial is wrong?
speaking.instructions:
Say each of these aloud and then say which dial is set wrongly.
I am writing to enquire about the position and I'd be dead keen to hear back.
Dear Sir or Madam, I need the figures. Yours sincerely.
We would be grateful if you could sort it out.
Please be advised that we can't do it.
I'd like to request the aforementioned data.
Record all five with your diagnoses.
In each one, most of the sentence is right and one part is not — that is what makes them hard to hear without checking dial by dial.
speaking.tutor: Say five mismatched sentences and ask the tutor which part is at the wrong level.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Say it both ways
speaking.instructions:
Say twelve phrases twice — once ending in a preposition, once with the formal alternative where one exists.
The department I work in / the department in which I work.
Include at least three where no alternative exists — look after, deal with, put up with, come across.
Record all of them.
Say aloud after each pair which one you would actually use, and for what document. Neither is wrong; only one fits.
speaking.tutor: Say six phrases ending in prepositions and ask the tutor for the formal alternative to each, then check which have none.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Three readers
speaking.instructions:
Take one real request you might need to make.
Say it three times: to a close colleague, to somebody in another department, and to an external organisation.
Each version should be thirty to sixty seconds.
Record all three.
Then listen back and check the dials in each. The most common failure is that the middle version drifts too close to one of the outer two.
speaking.tutor: Make the same request to the tutor three times at three levels and ask it to say who each version was for.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Summary aloud
speaking.instructions:
Take something you know well — a project, a problem, a process.
Say a one-sentence summary of it that would work if the listener heard nothing else.
It must contain the finding and the recommendation, not the subject.
Do this for four different things. Record all four.
After each, say the version that fails — this is about, this examines — and hear the difference. Describing the subject is what most summaries do.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor a four-sentence account and ask it to produce a one-sentence summary that could stand alone.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the three versions aloud
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read all three versions aloud.
Then say aloud: how the directness dial moves across the three, quoting the request from each.
Then say what the third version contains that the others do not, and why.
Then say whether the third is better writing than the first.
Record the last three parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Read the tutor the first version and ask it to rewrite it for an external body.

writing.title: Writing 1 — One request, three readers
writing.prompt:
Take one real request.
Write it three times, as in Reading 3.
Version A: to a close colleague. Three or four lines, contractions, direct.
Version B: to a colleague in another department. Email format with a subject line, moderate formality.
Version C: to an external organisation. Formal letter with the correct opening and closing pairing.
The request must be identical in all three.
Then write three lines: which dial moved most between A and C, what C contains that A does not and why, and which version you would find hardest to get right.
writing.model:
VERSION A — to a close colleague
Hi Sam — any chance you could dig out the March figures for the Eastbourne bay? Need them for Thursday. Ta.

VERSION B — to another department
Subject: March figures — Eastbourne bay
Hello Priya,
I'm putting together the quarterly summary and I need the March throughput figures for the Eastbourne bay. Would you be able to send them over by Wednesday? Thursday is when the summary goes to the board.
Thanks very much,
Dani

VERSION C — to an external body
Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing to request the throughput data recorded at the Eastbourne facility for the month of March. The information is required in connection with a quarterly review, and I would be grateful to receive it by Wednesday 26 April.
Please confirm whether any charge applies. I enclose a copy of our registration for reference.
Yours faithfully,
D. Okonkwo

1. Directness moved most. Any chance you could to would you be able to to I would be grateful to receive — three settings of the same dial.
2. C asks about charges and encloses a registration. An external body may charge and may need to verify who is asking; neither applies to a colleague.
3. B is hardest. A and C have clear conventions and B has none — it has to be warm without being casual, and it is the one I would most likely pitch wrongly.
writing.starter: VERSION A — to a close colleague
writing.criteria: The same request in all three; A uses contractions and is direct; B is in email format with a specific subject line; C uses the correct opening and closing pairing and no contractions; C contains at least one thing the others do not, for a stated reason; three lines of commentary
writing.support: Write B last. A and C have conventions to follow and B does not, which makes it the version most likely to drift towards one of the others.
writing.extension: Send version C's opening to somebody and ask them to guess the relationship. Then do the same with A's.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A summary that works alone
writing.prompt:
Take something you know well — a problem at work, a process, a project, an investigation.
Write a short report of it: summary, background, findings, conclusions, recommendations. About 250 words.
Write the summary last.
The summary must contain the findings and the recommendations, not a description of the report.
Then write two lines: what your first attempt at the summary said, and what you changed.
writing.model:
SUMMARY
Booking-in on Bay 2 takes about twenty-two minutes against a target of ten. Two causes account for most of the excess: a duplicated data entry that has existed since the system change in 2022, and a paper log that no longer matches the screens. Three changes are recommended, of which only the second requires any expenditure.

BACKGROUND
Booking-in was timed on twenty-two days between January and June, on days when the writer was on shift. The target of ten minutes dates from 2019 and has not been revised.

FINDINGS
The average was approximately twenty-two minutes. The same order reference is entered three times, twice on screen and once on paper. The paper log has four fields that no longer exist on the screens, and two screen fields that do not appear on paper. Delays were longer on days when agency staff were working, though the sample is too small to be confident about this.

CONCLUSIONS
The duplication accounts for most of the excess. The mismatch between paper and screen contributes and is separately a source of error.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Remove the second on-screen entry. No cost.
2. Reprint the paper log to match the current screens. About 200.
3. Retime after three months to confirm the effect.

1. My first summary said: this report examines booking-in times on Bay 2 and makes recommendations.
2. I changed it to state the actual figure, the two causes, and the fact that only one recommendation costs anything — because a reader who reads nothing else can now act.
writing.length: About 250 words in five sections plus two lines
writing.criteria: Five sections in the conventional order; the summary contains findings and recommendations rather than a description; recommendations follow from findings; at least one limitation acknowledged; two lines comparing the first and final summary
writing.support: Write the summary twice. The first attempt will describe the report; write it anyway, then write the second knowing that the reader may read only that.
writing.extension: Give somebody only your summary and ask what they would do. If they cannot say, it is still describing rather than reporting.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the three versions
writing.prompt:
Use the three versions in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Quote the request from each version and say how the directness dial moves.
2. Compare the openings and closings. Which pairing is fixed, and why does it matter?
3. What does version C contain that A and B do not, and why?
4. Is version C better writing than version A? Explain.
5. Rewrite version A as it would be sent to a colleague you have never met but who is at the same level as you.
writing.model:
1. Any chance you could dig out; would you be able to send them over; I would be grateful to receive it. Each step adds distance between the writer and the request — the first is barely a request at all, the second asks about ability, and the third states the writer's feeling rather than asking anything directly.
2. Dear Sir or Madam with Yours faithfully is the fixed pairing, and a name would require Yours sincerely instead. It matters because it is one of very few conventions in English correspondence that is genuinely rigid, and readers who write letters regularly notice immediately when it is wrong.
3. C asks whether any charge applies and encloses a copy of a registration. An external organisation may charge for data and may need to verify who is requesting it, neither of which arises with a colleague. The extra content follows from the relationship rather than from the register.
4. No. It is differently pitched, not better. Version A is entirely appropriate to a close colleague and version C would read as cold and strange if sent to Sam. A register too formal for the relationship is as noticeable as one too casual, and the assumption that the formal version is always the safe choice is wrong.
5. Model: Hello Priya — I don't think we've met; I'm Dani, in operations at Northfield. I'm putting together the quarterly summary and I need the March throughput figures for the Eastbourne bay. Would you be able to send them across by Wednesday? Thanks very much, Dani.
writing.starter: 1. Any chance you could dig out;
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 1 quotes all three and describes the movement; answer 3 attributes the extra content to the relationship rather than to style; answer 4 rejects the assumption that more formal is safer; answer 5 pitches between A and B and adds an introduction
writing.support: Underline the request in each version before answering. Everything else in the three documents varies too, and isolating the identical request is what makes the dial visible.
writing.extension: Write version C as an email rather than a letter. Which conventions change and which do not?

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the twelve
writing.prompt:
Every item has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. I am writing to enquire about the position and I'd be dead keen to hear back.
2. Dear Sir or Madam … Yours sincerely.
3. Dear Ms Bello … Yours faithfully.
4. Dear Sir or Madam … Best wishes. (a formal letter)
5. Hello Sam … Yours faithfully. (an email to a close colleague)
6. Please find attached a copy of the invoice. (a posted letter)
7. Subject: Query (an email about March figures for one site)
8. This report examines the causes of the delay. (as the whole summary)
9. I would be grateful if you could sort it out.
10. The department in which I work. (an email to a colleague)
11. The person after whom I look.
12. Please be advised that we can't do it.
writing.model:
1. …and I would be glad to hear from you. (Pattern 1 — the contraction and the colloquial phrase are at the wrong settings)
2. Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully. (Pattern 2 — no name takes faithfully)
3. Dear Ms Bello … Yours sincerely. (Pattern 2 — a name takes sincerely)
4. Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully. (Pattern 2 — best wishes is for email)
5. Hello Sam … Thanks / Best. (Pattern 2 — never Yours faithfully in an email)
6. Please find enclosed a copy of the invoice. (Pattern 2 — enclosed for post, attached for email)
7. Subject: March figures — Eastbourne bay. (Pattern 2 — a subject line says what it is about)
8. The delay had two causes, one of which recurs; three changes are recommended. (Pattern 2 — a summary reports, it does not describe)
9. I would be grateful if you could resolve this. (Pattern 1 — sort it out is colloquial in a formal frame)
10. The department I work in. (Pattern 3 — in which is stiff in an email to a colleague)
11. The person I look after. (Pattern 3 — look after cannot be separated)
12. Please be advised that we are unable to do so. (Pattern 1 — the contraction clashes with please be advised)
writing.criteria: All twelve corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 2, 3, 4 and 5 all fixed by the opening-and-closing pairing; number 10 fixed by making it less formal rather than more
writing.support: Numbers 2 to 5 are one convention four times. Write the two pairings at the top of your page — name takes sincerely, no name takes faithfully, and email takes neither — and all four fall out.
writing.extension: Number 10 is the only item fixed by reducing formality, which is the direction learners rarely try. Write two more like it.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which dial is wrong?
activities.instructions:
Each sentence has one dial at the wrong setting. Name the dial and fix it.
1. I am writing to enquire about the position and I'd be dead keen to hear back.
2. Please be advised that we can't do it.
3. I would be grateful if you could sort it out.
4. Dear Sir or Madam, I need the figures by Friday.
5. We regret to inform you that your thing didn't work out.
6. Kindly send over the stuff at your earliest convenience.
7. Further to our conversation, thanks a lot.
8. I'd like to request the aforementioned data.
9. Hi Priya, I am writing to enquire whether you would be able to furnish me with the March figures.
10. Pursuant to clause 6, can you sort this?
11. It is felt that the deadline is a bit rubbish.
12. We would be grateful if you could get back to us ASAP.
activities.answers:
1. Contractions and colloquial vocabulary — …and I would be glad to hear from you.
2. Contraction — …that we are unable to do so.
3. Vocabulary — …if you could resolve this.
4. Directness — I should be grateful if you could send me the figures by Friday.
5. Vocabulary — …that your application has been unsuccessful.
6. Vocabulary — kindly send the documents at your earliest convenience. (Stuff and over are both too casual for kindly.)
7. Vocabulary — further to our conversation, thank you.
8. Contraction — I would like to request the data. (Aforementioned is also unnecessary here.)
9. Vocabulary and structure — Hi Priya, could you send me the March figures?
10. Vocabulary and directness — pursuant to clause 6, please confirm the position.
11. Vocabulary — it is felt that the deadline may be optimistic.
12. Vocabulary — …if you could reply as soon as possible.
Every one has most of its dials correct. That is what makes them hard to hear — the sentence is not wrong, one part of it is pitched differently from the rest.
Number 9 goes the other way from the rest: the frame is casual and the language is over-formal, and the fix is to bring the language down rather than the frame up.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Conventions
activities.instructions:
Answer each in a full sentence.
1. You know the recipient's name. Opening and closing?
2. You do not know the name. Opening and closing?
3. Three closings for a professional email, warmest first.
4. What goes in an email subject line, and what does not?
5. Enclosed or attached — which for a letter, which for an email?
6. The conventional order of report sections.
7. When is a report summary written, and when is it read?
8. What must a summary contain?
9. What is wrong with: this report examines the causes of the delay?
10. What is the one thing that should never appear in a work email?
11. Where do recommendations come from?
12. Why state the scope before the findings?
activities.answers:
1. Dear Ms Bello, closing Yours sincerely.
2. Dear Sir or Madam, closing Yours faithfully.
3. Best wishes, kind regards, regards.
4. What the email is about, specifically enough to be found again later. Not Query, Hello, or the recipient's name.
5. Enclosed for a posted letter; attached for an email.
6. Summary, background, findings, conclusions, recommendations.
7. Written last and read first — and often it is the only part read.
8. The findings and the recommendations, so that somebody who reads nothing else can act.
9. It describes the report rather than reporting anything. A reader who read only that would know nothing.
10. Anything you would not want read aloud in a meeting. Email is written like speech and read like a document.
11. From the findings. A recommendation with no finding behind it is an opinion.
12. Because what was not examined shapes what the findings can support — the same point as methodology in Unit 17.
Numbers 1 to 5 are conventions and can simply be learned. Numbers 7 to 12 are judgements, and they are where reports actually fail.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Preposition at the end
activities.instructions:
Write the natural version and the formal alternative. Write NO ALTERNATIVE where there is none.
1. The department I work in.
2. The person I spoke to.
3. The person I look after.
4. The problem we are dealing with.
5. The situation we find ourselves in.
6. The report I came across.
7. The colleague I gave it to.
8. The delay we put up with.
9. The clause I was referring to.
10. The site the incident occurred at.
11. The system we rely on.
12. The figures I was asking about.
activities.answers:
1. The department in which I work.
2. The person to whom I spoke.
3. NO ALTERNATIVE — look after cannot be separated.
4. NO ALTERNATIVE — deal with cannot be separated.
5. The situation in which we find ourselves.
6. NO ALTERNATIVE — come across cannot be separated.
7. The colleague to whom I gave it.
8. NO ALTERNATIVE — put up with cannot be separated.
9. The clause to which I was referring.
10. The site at which the incident occurred.
11. The system on which we rely.
12. The figures about which I was asking. — grammatical and distinctly awkward; better to rewrite.
Four of the twelve have no formal alternative, and all four are multi-word verbs where the preposition is part of the meaning rather than attached to it.
Number 12 shows the third case: an alternative exists, it is correct, and it is worse. Rearranging to obey a rule that does not exist regularly produces sentences like that one.
Every natural version on the left is correct in any register, including a formal report.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Move it up, move it down
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each at the level indicated, changing only what needs to change.
1. Can you send me the figures? — to an external body.
2. I am writing to enquire regarding the aforementioned matter. — to a close colleague.
3. We need to get the data. — formal.
4. Please be advised that we are unable to comply. — to a colleague.
5. Tell us if anything changes. — formal.
6. Cheers for sorting that out. — to a client.
7. It is felt that the timescale may be optimistic. — to a close colleague.
8. Thanks a lot, speak soon. — to an external body.
activities.answers:
1. I would be grateful if you could send me the figures.
2. Hi — just wanted to ask about that thing we discussed.
3. We are required to obtain the data.
4. Sorry, we can't do that.
5. Please notify us of any change.
6. Thank you very much for dealing with that.
7. I think the deadline is too tight.
8. Thank you for your assistance. I look forward to hearing from you.
Numbers 2, 4 and 7 move downward, which is the direction learners practise least. Moving down is not simply removing formal words — it usually means saying the thing more directly, which some people find harder.
Number 7 is worth noticing: bringing it down restored the person. It is felt has no owner, and I think does.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Audit your own emails
activities.instructions:
Find five emails you have sent in the last month, to five different kinds of recipient.
For each, mark the five dials — vocabulary, contractions, structure, directness, personal — as high, medium or low.
Mark any email where one dial is out of step with the others.
Rewrite one.
Write two lines: which dial you set most consistently, and which you set by accident.
activities.answers:
No key — they are your emails.
What most people find: contractions are the dial they control deliberately, and directness is the one set by accident. Requests come out at whatever level the writer happened to feel, which varies with mood and with how well the day is going rather than with the recipient.
The second finding is about drift. Longer emails frequently start formal and end casual, because the writer relaxes as they go. The closing is often two settings below the opening, and it is the part the reader remembers.
The third finding is the useful one: almost everybody has one email in five where the register is wrong for the recipient, and it is usually too formal to somebody they know well rather than too casual to somebody they do not.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Find a stiff sentence
activities.instructions:
Find three real sentences in official writing where a preposition has been moved to avoid ending a clause — look for in which, to whom, of which, on which.
Copy each out.
Rewrite each with the preposition at the end.
Decide which version the document should have used, and why.
Write one line on whether the formal version was earning its place.
activities.answers:
No key — they are your sentences.
What most people find: in which and of which appear constantly in official writing and about half of them are earning their place. In a contract or a formal report, surrounded by long sentences and formal vocabulary, they fit. In a customer letter that is otherwise plain, they stand out.
The second finding is that to whom is rarer than the others and more often misplaced. It is the most formal of the group and it appears in documents whose other dials are set much lower, which is exactly the mismatch card 1 describes.
The third finding, which surprises people: you will find at least one sentence that has been rearranged into something genuinely worse — usually longer, occasionally ambiguous — in order to avoid a preposition at the end. That is the invented rule doing damage, and once you have seen an example the rule stops having any hold.

quizzes.q: How many dials does formality have, according to this unit?
quizzes.why: Vocabulary, contractions, sentence structure, directness and how personal the writing is. They move independently, which is why a document can be wrong while every word is right.

quizzes.q: What is wrong with: I am writing to enquire about the position and I'd be dead keen to hear back?
options: The contraction and the colloquial phrase clash with the formal opening
quizzes.a: The contraction and the colloquial phrase clash with the formal opening
quizzes.why: Every part is correct English. Three dials are set at different levels, and a reader notices immediately without necessarily being able to say why.

options: not necessarily long, vague or difficult
quizzes.a: not necessarily long, vague or difficult
quizzes.why: Length and abstraction are usually imprecision rather than formality. The most formal English at its best is precise.

quizzes.q: You do not know the recipient's name. Which closing?
quizzes.why: No name takes faithfully; a name takes sincerely. It is one of very few genuinely rigid conventions in English correspondence.

quizzes.q: Which never appears in a professional email?
quizzes.why: It belongs to letters only. Emails close with best wishes, kind regards or regards, in roughly descending order of warmth.

quizzes.q: When is a report summary written, and when read?
quizzes.why: In most professional contexts it is the only part read, which is why it must work alone.

quizzes.q: What is wrong with a summary that says this report examines the causes of the delay?
options: It describes the report instead of reporting anything
It should be at the end
quizzes.a: It describes the report instead of reporting anything
quizzes.why: A reader who read only that would know nothing. A summary must contain the findings and the recommendations.

quizzes.q: Where did the rule against ending a sentence with a preposition come from?
options: Seventeenth-century writers who thought English should behave like Latin
It has always been part of English
quizzes.a: Seventeenth-century writers who thought English should behave like Latin
quizzes.why: Latin genuinely cannot do it. English always has, and every major writer in the language has done it.

quizzes.q: The person I spoke to and the person to whom I spoke are...
options: both correct — the second is more formal
quizzes.a: both correct — the second is more formal
quizzes.why: It is a register choice rather than a correctness question. To whom belongs in formal documents and sounds affected in speech.

quizzes.q: Why can you not say the person after whom I look?
options: Look after is a single unit of meaning and cannot be separated
quizzes.a: Look after is a single unit of meaning and cannot be separated
quizzes.why: This is a real constraint, unlike the invented rule, and it applies to deal with, put up with and come across as well.

quizzes.q: Version C of the request in Reading 3 asks about charges. Why?
options: An external body may charge, which does not arise with a colleague
quizzes.a: An external body may charge, which does not arise with a colleague
quizzes.why: The extra content follows from the relationship rather than from the register — formality is not the only thing that changes between readers.

quizzes.q: Is the most formal version always the safest choice?
options: No — too formal for the relationship is as noticeable as too casual
quizzes.a: No — too formal for the relationship is as noticeable as too casual
quizzes.why: Version C sent to a close colleague would read as cold and strange. Learners often treat maximum formality as safe, and it is not.

teacherNotes.note: Three pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key or an explicit no-key note with a what-most-people-find finding. Practice 1 is the diagnostic and every item has most of its dials set correctly, which is what makes register errors hard to hear — the sentence is not wrong, one part of it is pitched differently from the rest.

Teaching formality as a single scale is why learners produce documents that are wrong while every word in them is right. Separating the dials makes the error locatable and the check mechanical — go through five things one at a time rather than asking whether something feels formal enough. Speaking 1 moves one dial at a time deliberately, so each becomes audible on its own.

This belief produces exactly the writing Units 4 and 8 taught learners to dismantle, and naming it here closes that loop. It is worth stating plainly that the most formal registers at their best are precise, and that length and abstraction are usually imprecision rather than professionalism. Practice 4 asks learners to move sentences down as well as up, which is the direction they practise least.

teacherNotes.type: The preposition rule is invented and worth saying so
teacherNotes.note: Learners taught the rule apply it anxiously and produce stiff or ungrammatical sentences. Naming its seventeenth-century Latin origin removes the anxiety in a way that saying it is fine does not. Practice 3 includes four items with no formal alternative at all, which is the practical argument: obeying the rule sometimes forces a writer into something that is not English.

teacherNotes.type: The summary is the part that fails
teacherNotes.note: Conventions like sincerely and faithfully can simply be learned. The report summary is a judgement and it is where reports actually fail — most summaries describe the document rather than reporting anything, and the summary is often the only part read. Writing 2 asks learners to write it twice and to record what their first attempt said, because the first attempt is almost always descriptive.

teacherNotes.type: Too formal is also an error
teacherNotes.note: Learners treat maximum formality as the safe default, and Reading 3's third comprehension question and Writing 3 question 4 both address this directly. Version C sent to a close colleague reads as cold and strange. Practice 5's key finds that most people's one mispitched email in five is too formal to somebody they know rather than too casual to somebody they do not.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Practice 5 asks learners to audit five emails they have actually sent, and Writing 2 asks for a report about a real workplace situation: the content of those emails, the recipients, the employer and any operational detail must never be collected, shared or entered into the app. Practice 5 asks only for dial settings, not for the text. Practice 6 uses public official writing, which carries no such concern.

selfAssessment.statement: I can tell which part of a sentence is at the wrong level of formality.
I can pair Dear Sir or Madam with Yours faithfully and write a summary that works alone.
I can say the person I spoke to without thinking it is wrong.
I can write the same request three ways and know which one fits the situation.

assignment.title: One request at three levels, and a report that can be read in one paragraph
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record the same request three times — to a close colleague, to another department, and to an external body — then record four one-sentence summaries that would each work if nothing else were heard, saying after each the failed version that only describes the subject. Second, write the three versions from Writing 1 with the three lines of commentary, write the five-section report from Writing 2 with the summary written last and the two lines comparing your drafts, and add your full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3. Keep everything together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written work
